issues.legal_issue: A court exercising certiorari jurisdiction may not reappraise evidence and substitute its factual findings for supported findings of lower authorities unless a recognized ground for certiorari is established.
material_facts: Both lower authorities found on the evidence that a person who was not a member of the tenant’s family sat in the shop and conducted the tenant’s business on the tenant’s behalf.
The reviewing court rejected that finding after reassessing the evidence, including a commissioner’s report to which an objection remained undecided.
The lower authorities’ findings rested on evidence, and no jurisdictional error, breach of natural justice, or manifest or apparent error of law justified disturbing them.
issues.conclusion: The reviewing court exceeded its jurisdiction by reappraising the evidence; its order was set aside and the lower authorities’ orders were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, certiorari may issue where an inferior tribunal or subordinate court has committed an error of jurisdiction, breached natural justice, or made a manifest or apparent error of law. It does not authorize reappraisal of evidence without sufficient legal reason or substitution of contrary factual findings. The commissioner’s report, because an objection to it remained undecided, was not a final document and could not be relied upon as it stood. No earlier case was cited for this principle.

rule.if: certiorari_proceeding and supported_lower_fact_findings and no_recognized_certiorari_error and reviewing_court_reappraised_evidence

predicates.certiorari_proceeding: A party sought judicial review of a lower authority’s decision by a writ in the nature of certiorari.
predicates.supported_lower_fact_findings: The lower authorities made factual findings that rested on evidence.
predicates.no_recognized_certiorari_error: The lower authorities’ decision did not suffer from a jurisdictional error, a breach of natural justice, or a manifest or apparent error of law.
predicates.reviewing_court_reappraised_evidence: The reviewing court reassessed the evidence and reached factual findings contrary to those of the lower authorities.
predicates.reappraisal_exceeds_jurisdiction: The reviewing court’s reappraisal of the evidence exceeded its jurisdiction.

issues.definition: When a reviewing court considers a certiorari proceeding, supported factual findings below, no recognized certiorari error, and a reappraisal of evidence, the rule treats that reappraisal as exceeding jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A person who occupies premises as the tenant’s agent and conducts the tenant’s business on the tenant’s behalf does not thereby cause the tenant to be deemed to have ceased occupying the premises merely because the agent is not a member of the tenant’s family.
material_facts: The lower authorities found that the tenant continued the vegetable-selling business in the shop and that a person who was not a member of the tenant’s family sat there and conducted the business on the tenant’s behalf.
The landlord alleged that the tenant had ceased to occupy the shop and had allowed it to be occupied by others, but the lower authorities found subletting unproved.
The reviewing court treated the non-family member’s presence as occupation by that person and held the premises deemed vacant.
issues.conclusion: The agent’s conduct of the business on the tenant’s behalf counted as occupation by the tenant, so the premises were not deemed vacant on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 12(1)(b) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, a tenant is deemed to have ceased to occupy a building if the tenant has allowed it to be occupied by a person who is not a member of the tenant’s family. Occupation by a person acting as the tenant’s agent is not occupation of the kind contemplated by that provision; when a person carries on business in the premises on behalf of and for the original occupant, the premises are treated as occupied by that occupant. Smt. Keshar Bai v. District Judge, Mathura was distinguished because it did not specifically consider the scope of “occupied” in relation to an agent.

predicates.rent_control_vacancy_determination: A proceeding sought to determine whether premises were deemed vacant under a rent-control scheme.
predicates.nonfamily_person_present: A person who was not a member of the tenant’s family was present in the premises.
predicates.person_operated_business_for_tenant: That person conducted the tenant’s business in the premises on behalf of and for the tenant.
predicates.no_deemed_vacancy_from_agent_occupation: The tenant is not deemed to have ceased occupying the premises solely because the agent conducted the tenant’s business there.

issues.definition: In a rent-control vacancy determination, when a non-family member is present and conducts the tenant’s business on the tenant’s behalf, the premises are not deemed vacant from that agent’s occupation.
